subject: Business Models
title: Medieval Banking
description: A short lesson to help you apply Medieval Banking.

hook.text: The Medici family of Florence became Europe's most powerful bankers in the 1400s.

buildup.text: They invented the 'bill of exchange'—a way to transfer money across borders without carrying gold.

discovery.text: This was effectively the first wire transfer. A letter replaced a dangerous wagon full of coins.

twist.text: Church law banned charging interest. Bankers disguised it as 'fees' or currency conversion charges.

climax.text: Banking made long-distance commerce possible. Without credit, global trade couldn't scale.

punchline.text: The Medicis moved money with paper, not wagons.

quiz.question: What did the 'bill of exchange' replace?

details.summary: Medieval banking emerged in Italian city-states as merchant families like the Medici developed deposit banking, letters of credit, double-entry bookkeeping, and international branch networks..
details.whyItMatters: Italian medieval banks created the financial infrastructure that powered the Renaissance and enabled European global expansion..
takeaways: Italian merchant families like the Medici invented modern deposit banking
Letters of credit eliminated the need to transport gold across dangerous routes
International branch networks enabled commerce across countries and currencies

faq.question: How did medieval banks work around the religious ban on usury?
faq.answer: The Catholic Church prohibited charging interest on loans. Banks charged foreign exchange fees instead of interest, embedded charges in complex currency conversion transactions, classified returns as risk-sharing rather than interest, and structured deals as partnerships rather than loans.

faq.question: What innovations did the Medici bank introduce?
faq.answer: A decentralized branch network in major European commercial centers, each operating as a separate legal partnership. This limited the parent bank's liability if a branch failed. They also pioneered sophisticated accounting, foreign exchange trading, and credit instruments for the papacy.
